questions.q: What does linearizability guarantee?
options: Each operation appears to take effect atomically between its start and end
All transactions execute as if in some serial order, with concurrent ones freely reordered
All replicas converge to the same value once writes stop arriving
A client always reads values at least as new as ones it previously read

questions.q: What does eventual consistency promise?
options: Reads always return the latest acknowledged write within one second
Writes become visible to all clients in the order they were issued
Conflicting writes are impossible because replicas serialize them
Absent new writes, replicas eventually converge to the same value

questions.q: What does read-your-writes guarantee for a single user?
options: Their reads reflect every other user's latest writes immediately
After they write, their own subsequent reads include that write
Their writes are durable across datacenter failures
Their reads never block, even during network partitions

questions.q: Which anomaly does monotonic reads prevent?
options: Two different users permanently seeing writes in different orders
A write being lost after it was acknowledged
A user seeing a value, then later seeing an older one
A transaction reading its own uncommitted data

questions.q: What does causal consistency ensure?
options: All writes are seen in an identical order by every replica
Reads always reflect true real-time ordering across every client in the system globally
Only writes originating from the same client are ever ordered
Causally related writes are seen in order; concurrent writes may differ

questions.q: Which of these consistency models is the strongest?
options: Linearizability
Causal consistency
Eventual consistency
Monotonic reads

questions.q: Linearizability and serializability apply to what, respectively?
options: Batch jobs vs interactive queries
Reads vs writes on one replica
Single-object operations vs multi-object transactions
In-memory caching layers vs durable on-disk storage engines

questions.q: Why do systems offer weaker consistency models at all?
options: Weak consistency simplifies application code for developers
Lower latency and higher availability, especially across regions
Strong consistency requires specialized atomic clocks in every datacenter
Weaker models let replicas skip durability, saving disk writes

questions.q: A user posts a comment, refreshes, and it is gone, reappearing later. Which minimal session guarantee fixes this?
options: Monotonic writes on the feed service
Serializable isolation in the database
Read-your-writes for that user's session
Linearizability across all users' sessions

questions.q: Reading a lagging replica right after writing to the primary breaks read-your-writes. Common fix?
options: Disable replication until the user's session terminates
Pin the user's reads to the primary (or a caught-up replica) briefly after their writes
Use a faster serialization format between primary and replicas
Retry every read up to three separate times and return the oldest value observed across attempts

questions.q: Two users see a chat thread as A-then-B vs B-then-A, where B replies to A. Which model rules this out?
options: Eventual consistency, since both users' views eventually converge anyway
Monotonic reads applied on each user's device
Read-your-writes for both message authors
Causal consistency, since the reply depends on the original

questions.q: What do quorum reads and writes (R + W > N) in Dynamo-style stores actually give you?
options: Reads overlap the latest write's replica set, though not full linearizability without extra care
Fully serializable multi-key ACID transactions spanning arbitrary sets of keys and concurrent clients
Guaranteed causal ordering across all keys and all clients
Exactly-once write semantics without any client retries

questions.q: Why does linearizability get expensive across geographic regions?
options: Data must be re-encrypted at every regional boundary crossing
Agreement on write order requires round trips that pay cross-region latency
Each region must permanently store a full duplicate copy of every other region's logs
Clock skew forces all regions to pause writes whenever clocks drift

questions.q: A user's profile photo alternates between old and new on successive requests. Which minimal guarantee stops this?
options: Write-ahead logging at the primary database
Causal consistency between unrelated users' sessions
Monotonic reads, e.g., by pinning the session to one replica
Strict serializability for all photo upload transactions

questions.q: With serializability but not linearizability, which anomaly is still allowed?
options: A later transaction reading state older than one that committed before it in real time
Two transactions both committing conflicting writes to one row
A transaction reading another transaction's uncommitted intermediate state
Lost updates whenever two concurrent increments race on the very same counter row

questions.q: CRDTs are designed for which setting?
options: Single-leader replication deployments that need faster automatic failover
Strongly consistent SQL transactions running on one node
Deterministic scheduling of threads within one process
Multi-writer replication where concurrent updates merge without coordination

questions.q: A ledger does check-balance-then-deduct against eventually consistent replicas. What is the risk?
options: Deducts become progressively slower over time as replicas struggle to converge
Two concurrent deducts can both pass the stale check, overdrawing the account
The ledger loses durability because convergence deletes history
Reads block indefinitely while waiting for all replicas to agree

questions.q: Chain: client, cache, strongly consistent DB with replicas. Users still report stale reads. Likely culprit?
options: The cache serves entries written before the latest DB update, outside the DB's guarantees
The primary demotes itself during backups, losing acknowledged writes
The replicas acknowledge incoming writes before the primary has actually committed them
TCP reordering delivers responses out of order to the client

questions.q: A geo-replicated store offers per-key linearizability. What can still go wrong across keys?
options: Single-key reads can return values that were never written
A single key's version history can fork permanently and irreparably between two regions
Reads of one individual key can travel backwards in time
Cross-key invariants can be observed violated, since ordering is not transactional

questions.q: A client sees its own write on one read, then misses it on the next read from a different replica. Which two guarantees are violated?
options: Monotonic writes and causal consistency
Write-follows-reads and linearizability
Read-your-writes and monotonic reads
Serializability and durability
